title: Compassion Benchmark Daily Briefing — September 24, 2026 (A Wage Court Moves a Score Up, and a $40 Million Verdict Moves One Down)
headline: Progressive's score was never checked before — a $40 million jury verdict is the first real measurement.
summary:
This is a catch-up cycle. It widens the usual 14-day lookback to 15 days specifically to cover September 23, the one day this month no earlier check ever reached. No event dated only to September 23 turned up — a real finding about coverage, not a gap in the search.

Twenty-one organizations were checked. Four proposed score changes came out of it, and three of the four are first-ever measurements: Progressive, Unum Group and Abu Dhabi had never been individually checked before tonight, so their published numbers were placeholders, not prior findings. Only Australia is a genuine re-measurement against a real earlier check.

Progressive's published 76.3 falls to a proposed 36.9 after a federal jury in Oklahoma found the insurer acted in bad faith denying a driver's claim and awarded $40 million in damages — a court finding, not an accusation, though Progressive is appealing and the judgment is not final. Unum Group's published 60.9 falls to a proposed 39.4 on a court-approved $14.8 million settlement: the disability insurer underpaid the very staff who decide whether disabled people get paid. Australia's published 62.5 falls to a proposed 48.8 on a Human Rights Watch report marking 25 years of offshore detention on Nauru and Manus Island, alongside a real prior baseline from April.

Abu Dhabi's published 21.9 rises to a proposed 28.1 — the night's one upward finding. An emirate labor court recovered $2.1 million in unpaid wages for 948 workers. The finding is held for review rather than filed as a confirmed upgrade only because every figure behind it comes from UAE government or UAE-owned sources with no independent audit located.

One finding was measured but not filed at all: Tronox would measure 13.7 points above its published score, using the identical math as a real change applied in July to a different company, Freeport-McMoRan, starting from the identical published number. Tronox's published number turns out to be shared, digit for digit, with two companies that no longer exist. That match is treated as one question about the benchmark's own placeholder data, not as grounds to file Tronox alone.

Three readings held: West Virginia (a state that published its own child-fatality failures, which raised its transparency reading), China (a new travel-ban decree, evidence too thin so far to move a score that is already near the bottom of the index), and Djibouti (a real open border for Yemeni refugees, already credited, mostly funded by others).

Release watch: 0 sources registered — detection did not run.

topSignals.title: A Wage Court Moved a Score Up — the Same Rigor That Catches Harm Also Has to Credit Repair
topSignals.whyItMatters: An instrument that only ever finds harm isn't measuring anything. This is the same evidence standard, applied to money a court actually returned to workers.
topSignals.description:
Abu Dhabi's published score of 21.9 out of 100 had never been individually checked before this cycle. A first review proposes 28.1 — still Developing band, no tier change, but the largest upward finding in recent cycles.

The reason: on September 21, 2026, the Abu Dhabi Labour Court — a court inside the emirate's own judicial department, not a federal UAE body — was reported to have recovered about $2.1 million (AED 7.8 million) in unpaid wages for 948 workers across three resolved cases. 457 workers were paid in full; 491 more are on structured payment plans.

The finding is held for review rather than confirmed as an upgrade for one reason: every figure behind it comes from the UAE government or UAE-owned outlets (The National, Arabian Business, Gulf News), and no independent audit was located to confirm the numbers. Set against that positive finding, Human Rights Watch's 2026 World Report on the UAE documents that employers still hold outsized control over migrant workers under the kafala sponsorship system, that trade unions remain banned, and that there is no minimum wage that applies to everyone equally. Both findings are real and both are counted.

evidence.quote: Full payments were secured for 457 workers, while 491 others received partial payments, with remaining balances placed under structured instalment plans.
evidence.claim: The Abu Dhabi Labour Court recovered roughly $2.1 million in unpaid wages for 948 workers across three resolved collective disputes.
Abu Dhabi recovered AED 7.81 million (about $2.13 million) for 948 workers across three collective labour cases resolved within three months.

Employers retain disproportionate control under the kafala sponsorship system; workers who leave abusive jobs risk false absconding charges leading to detention and deportation; trade unions remain banned and there is no non-discriminatory minimum wage.
evidence.source: Human Rights Watch, World Report 2026 (United Arab Emirates)

topSignals.title: A $40 Million Jury Verdict Is Progressive's First Real Measurement
topSignals.whyItMatters: Progressive's published score was never checked. A federal jury's finding of bad faith — not an accusation, a verdict — is the first hard evidence the benchmark has on the company.
topSignals.description:
Progressive's published score of 76.3 out of 100 had never been individually measured; six of its eight published dimensions sat at an identical, unchecked 4.0. A first measurement proposes 36.9, two tiers lower.

On September 11, 2026, a federal jury in the Northern District of Oklahoma found Progressive breached its duty of good faith handling a driver's claim for $25,000 in underinsured-motorist benefits, awarding $20 million in compensatory damages and $20 million in punitive damages. The jury heard evidence that Progressive's adjusters "lacked a basic understanding of how to handle Oklahoma underinsured motorist claims" and were paid under a company-wide profit-sharing program tied to cutting claim costs — a structural incentive, not one employee's mistake.

The judgment is not final. Progressive is seeking post-verdict relief in Tulsa federal court and an appeal is expected, which is why the measurement does not credit the company for repairing the harm yet. Genuine strength is also counted: Progressive ranked #19 on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For in 2026, a ninth consecutive year, and #1 on Forbes's list for employer culture from a 217,000-worker survey.

evidence.quote: Progressive's adjusters lacked a basic understanding of how to handle Oklahoma underinsured motorist claims
evidence.claim: Trial evidence established a company-wide adjuster competence gap in Oklahoma claims handling.
evidence.source: Repairer Driven News, reporting the N.D. Okla. jury verdict

evidence.quote: policyholders are not simply a means to collect premiums and increase corporate profit
evidence.claim: The court's framing of the verdict describes a decision pattern contradicting Progressive's stated values.
evidence.source: Repairer Driven News, reporting the N.D. Okla. jury verdict

evidence.claim: Progressive is seeking post-verdict relief in Tulsa federal court; the judgment is not final.

topSignals.title: Unum's First Measurement Turns on Who It Underpaid
topSignals.whyItMatters: A court found a disability insurer underpaid the staff who decide disability claims. That is the sharpest kind of finding — it is the company's own workforce, adjudicated, not alleged.
topSignals.description:
Unum Group's published score of 60.9 out of 100 had never been individually checked; it sits on a starting vector identical to three other insurers (The Hartford, Travelers, MetLife). A first measurement proposes 39.4, two tiers lower.

On April 17, 2025, a federal court in Tennessee gave final approval to a $14.8 million wage-and-hour settlement. The class: about 910 Unum disability benefits specialists — the employees who process claims and decide whether disabled people get paid — who said they were wrongly classified as exempt from overtime pay. Roughly 52 of them received more than $30,000 each.

Real strength is counted too: Unum's return-to-work and vocational rehabilitation programs, designed to restore a claimant's earning capacity, score as the single strongest finding in the assessment. And history is kept separate from today: a 2004 settlement with 48 states, which forced Unum to reassess 200,000 disability claims, is recorded as real but compelled reform, not current conduct.

evidence.claim: On April 17, 2025, the Eastern District of Tennessee granted final approval of a $14.8 million wage-and-hour class settlement covering about 910 Unum disability benefits specialists who alleged they were misclassified as exempt and denied overtime; participating members averaged over $10,000 each.
evidence.source: McGillivary Steele Elkin LLP, reporting the court order

evidence.claim: Unum and its workers agreed to a $14.8 million settlement to end the wage suit.

topSignals.title: Australia's Re-Check Weighs 25 Years of Offshore Detention Against Its Own Transparency
topSignals.whyItMatters: This is the one genuine re-measurement of the night, not a first check — real prior evidence plus a fresh Human Rights Watch report moved the number.
topSignals.description:
Australia's published score of 62.5 out of 100 falls to a proposed 48.8, crossing from the benchmark's Established tier into its Functional tier. Unlike tonight's other three proposed changes, this one rests partly on a real earlier baseline, not purely on an unchecked placeholder.

Human Rights Watch marked 25 years of Australia's offshore detention system on September 10, 2026: more than 5,000 people transferred to Nauru and Manus Island since 2001, at least 14 deaths since 2012, and an estimated $1.8 billion paid to Nauru to permanently accept people Australia turns away. Eight days later, Australia's Home Affairs Minister announced 100 more compliance officers and 250 new detention beds, a measure a rights group warned could deter exploited workers without papers from ever reporting abuse.

Australia is also credited for real transparency: its own Productivity Commission published data in July showing 4 of 19 Indigenous-outcome targets are getting worse — a government publishing its own bad news, counted as a genuine strength even as the overall score falls. A widely circulated figure of roughly 350 deportations to Nauru could not be confirmed by either primary source and was left out of the measurement.

evidence.quote: to accept people whom Australia rejects and expels
evidence.claim: Nauru was paid an estimated $1.8 billion to become a permanent endpoint for people Australia refuses.

evidence.quote: Mentally, I lost everything, I lost my golden age, I lost my health, lost my time
evidence.claim: A refugee describes the cumulative harm of offshore detention and rolling short-term visas.
Of 19 Closing the Gap Indigenous-outcome targets, 1 is met, 3 are on track, 5 are improving but off track and 4 are worsening — published by the government's own agency.

topSignals.title: A Company That No Longer Exists Shares Tronox's Starting Score — So Tronox's Finding Was Not Filed
topSignals.whyItMatters: The same math the benchmark applied to a different company in July reappeared tonight on Tronox. That repeat is evidence the number belongs to the benchmark's own unmeasured data, not to either company.
topSignals.description:
Tronox measured 32.5 out of 100 tonight, 13.7 points above its published 18.8 and a tier higher — but no change was proposed. The finding is recorded and set aside for a wider review instead.

The reason: Tronox's published 18.8 is shared, digit for digit across all eight measured behaviors, with Penn Virginia and Rex Energy — two companies checked this same cycle and found to no longer exist as independent public companies. A number one live company shares with two dissolved companies cannot be a measurement of the live one.

The match runs deeper. In July 2026, the benchmark applied the identical move — 18.8 up to 32.5, a 13.7-point rise — to a different company, Freeport-McMoRan, starting from the identical published number. Two independent measurements, five months apart, landing on the exact same number from the exact same start, is strong evidence the starting number itself is the problem. Filing Tronox alone would fix that same underlying number one company at a time instead of all at once, so tonight's finding is being routed to a review of the whole group of never-checked Fortune 500 companies in the benchmark's lowest tier.

evidence.claim: Tronox's published dimensions are byte-identical to Penn Virginia's and Rex Energy's; this cycle independently established that Penn Virginia ceased to exist as a company in 2023 and Rex Energy sold substantially all its assets in 2018.

In July 2026 the benchmark applied a +13.7-point upgrade to Freeport-McMoRan, from 18.8 to 32.5 — the identical starting value and identical delta this cycle's independent Tronox measurement produced.

sectorAlerts.sector: Fortune 500 — Two Insurers Get Their First Real Measurement, Both Fall
sectorAlerts.headline: Progressive and Unum Group both had first-ever checks tonight; both landed well below their never-measured published scores.
observations: Progressive (76.3 published, 36.9 proposed): a $40 million bad-faith jury verdict, not yet final, is the first hard evidence checked against a placeholder score.
Unum Group (60.9 published, 39.4 proposed): a court-approved $14.8 million settlement found the company underpaid its own disability-claims staff.

Against already-checked insurers (State Farm 13.8, Cigna 20.3, Centene 32.8, Humana 35.2), both proposed values still sit above the pack — but the direction is consistently downward whenever an insurer placeholder gets its first real check.

sectorAlerts.sector: Fortune 500 — A Placeholder Match Repeats a July Pattern Exactly
sectorAlerts.headline: Tronox's finding matches a real change applied in July to a different company, down to the exact number.
observations: Tronox measured 13.7 points above its published 18.8 — the identical delta the benchmark applied to Freeport-McMoRan in July from the identical starting number.
Tronox's published vector is shared, digit for digit, with Penn Virginia and Rex Energy, both confirmed this cycle to no longer exist as independent companies.
No change was filed for Tronox; the finding is routed to a review of the whole never-checked Critical-band Fortune 500 cluster instead.

sectorAlerts.sector: Countries — One Real Re-Check, Two Confirmations Near the Floor
sectorAlerts.headline: Australia's score falls on a real re-measurement; China and Djibouti both held near the bottom of the index.
observations: Australia (62.5 published, 48.8 proposed): a Human Rights Watch report marking 25 years of offshore detention, weighed against the country's own transparent reporting on its Indigenous-outcome gaps.

China (19.5 published, confirmed): a new travel-restriction decree was reviewed, but one nine-day-old source was not enough to move a founder-approved baseline that sits half a point from the next band.

Djibouti (17.5 published, confirmed): a genuine open-border response to nearly 3,000 Yemeni arrivals, already credited in an earlier measurement and mostly funded by international agencies rather than Djibouti itself.

sectorAlerts.sector: Global Cities — The Night's One Upward Finding, Held for Review
sectorAlerts.headline: Abu Dhabi's labor court recovered real money for real workers — the finding is held for review, not confirmed, pending independent verification.
observations: Abu Dhabi (21.9 published, 28.1 proposed): an emirate labor court recovered about $2.1 million in unpaid wages for 948 workers, attributable cleanly to city-level, not federal, conduct.
The finding is held rather than confirmed because every figure behind it comes from UAE government or UAE-owned sources, with no independent audit located.
Countervailing evidence — a banned trade-union system and no universal minimum wage, per Human Rights Watch — keeps the overall reading in the Developing band even as it rises.

sectorAlerts.sector: US States — Self-Disclosure of Failure Is Still Counted as a Strength
sectorAlerts.headline: West Virginia's own report on child-fatality failures raised its score, because publishing bad news honestly is itself measured.
observations: West Virginia (35.6 published, 36.9 confirmed): the state's own annual report disclosed 12 child deaths from abuse or neglect and named two specific corrective programs, raising its transparency reading.
The deaths themselves are outside this cycle's window and are not scored as new conduct; only the act of disclosing them, and the state's disaster-response request, fall inside it.

methodologyNotes.name: A Never-Checked Score Moving Is Not the Same as a Decline
methodologyNotes.description: Three of tonight's four proposed changes — Progressive, Unum Group and Abu Dhabi — had never been individually measured before this cycle. Their published scores were starting placeholders, not prior research findings. A first measurement correcting a placeholder describes what the benchmark did not yet know, not what the organization did differently this week.

methodologyNotes.name: An Instrument That Only Finds Harm Isn't Measuring Anything
methodologyNotes.description: Abu Dhabi's labor-court finding is scored with the same evidence bar as any downgrade: the underlying facts are held to flag-for-review rather than confirmed upgrade specifically because the sourcing is entirely government-adjacent. Crediting real positive conduct, at the same evidentiary standard used to catch harm, is treated as core to the benchmark's integrity, not an exception to it.

methodologyNotes.name: A Repeated Delta From an Identical Placeholder Is a Single Question, Not a Second Finding
methodologyNotes.description: Tronox measured the identical 13.7-point rise from the identical 18.8 starting value that a real change applied to a different company, Freeport-McMoRan, in July. Because Tronox's published number is also shared with two companies that no longer exist, the repeat is read as evidence about the benchmark's own unmeasured starting data, not about either company's conduct, and is routed to a cohort-wide review rather than filed as an individual change.

methodologyNotes.name: Court Verdicts Are Weighed Differently From Pending Allegations
methodologyNotes.description: Progressive's measurement rests on an adjudicated federal jury verdict, not an accusation still working through the courts. The verdict is not yet final — Progressive is appealing — so the benchmark credits no repair for it yet, but the underlying finding of bad faith is treated as decided fact, at the highest evidence tier the methodology uses.

forwardTriggers.trigger: The outcome of Progressive's post-verdict appeal in Tulsa federal court is the next test for its Accountability and Integrity reading.
A coordinator-level review of the never-checked Critical-band Fortune 500 cluster Tronox shares with Penn Virginia, Rex Energy and Sanchez Energy is the next step.
Independent verification of the AED 7.8 million wage-recovery figures would resolve whether this finding becomes a confirmed upgrade.
A UN treaty-body communication on the new exit-ban decree, or a documented individual case, is the next test for a score sitting half a point from the next band.

dailyOpeningQuestion.text: Tronox and Freeport-McMoRan share an identical published 18.8 placeholder vector and an identical measured +13.7 delta, yet Freeport-McMoRan's rise was applied in July while Tronox's is withheld this cycle — does a band-wide Critical-cluster review resolve that asymmetry, or does the next matching placeholder test screening rule five again, one company at a time?
dailyOpeningQuestion.tensionFraming: Two companies share an identical placeholder vector and an identical measured delta, but only one of them has ever had its rise applied.
